newsitem.title: USA: Helicopter ride yields images of N.Dakota disaster.
newsitem.headline: Helicopter ride yields images of N.Dakota disaster.

text.p: Grand Forks, seen from the air, is a ghost town that sits inside a vast chocolate swamp.
Some single-family homes have been reduced to little more than grey and red pyramids -- only their sloping roofs visible above the muddy floodwaters of the Red River.
Other houses are more lucky and cling precariously to patches of dry ground.
Journalists taken aloft in a National Guard helicopter got a full view of the devastation that has hit this city of 50,000 people which battled the "Great Flood of 1997" -- and lost.

A few lazy plumes of smoke waft up from three city blocks in the downtown area scarred this weekend by a vicious fire, which had firefighters vainly feeling below the floodwaters in a search for a working hydrant.
As the chopper hovers a few hundred feet above the burned-out husks, the smell of smoke pierces the cold air.
Black soot and a rosy powder stick to the charred buildings, the reddish film the remnant of chemical retardant that was dumped on the blaze Saturday by an airplane.

It is impossible to tell where the river once lay. The brown lake appears to extend for miles. The only clue to the speed of its current is a white recreational vehicle bobbing idly through what might have been a wheat field.

Seen from above, a thin line of shiny plastic runs through one otherwise smooth stretch of water -- the top edge of a makeshift sandbag and clay dike that volunteers mistakenly thought would hold back the flood.
Old Victorian-style homes in what was a wealthy neighbourhood look like mediaeval castles complete with their own moats. Only, the moats go on and on.
The steel girder midsections of three bridges are still visible, but their access ramps descend into the murky waters.

A green military truck carrying white plastic sandbags moves incongruously below, creating a long v-shaped wake that cuts through the brown water. Apart from the truck and a Coast Guard dinghy, the city is eerily still and motionless.

Seen from high overhead, there is just a patchwork of snow left on the ground. It's a bright, sunny day and the temperature reads 58 degrees Farenheit, but the white mounds linger from a punishing winter that dropped twice the normal amount of snow on this state.
The flood is the result of that snow -- and of a winter which will scar Grand Forks for a long time to come.
